The authors developed a custom-built extruder with a torque sensor to measure the extrusion force in real-time.
The extrusion force is used as feedback in a closed-loop control system to continuously adapt the material flow rate.
The authors demonstrate a strong linear correlation between the measured extrusion force and the width of the deposited line, with an R^2 of 0.99.
Force Controlled Printing (FCP) can deposit lines of desired width over a wide range of 33% up to 233% of the nozzle diameter.
FCP outperforms conventional feed-forward extrusion in print quality and disturbance rejection, while requiring little tuning and automatically adapting to changes in hardware settings.
With no adaptation, FCP can deposit lines of desired width under severe disturbances in bed leveling, such as layer heights ranging from 20% to 200% of the nominal height.
The authors use Liquid Crystal Polymers (LCPs) as the feedstock material, which self-assemble into nematic domains and align during extrusion, conferring exceptional mechanical properties.
The custom extruder design rigidly connects the hot end to the printer body, maintaining the same printing quality as a standard extruder.
The PID controller used in FCP includes two derivative terms: one for fast disturbances from the machine motion system, and one for slower disturbances from the filament extrusion system.
At very low layer heights (less than 50 μm), the linear relationship between reaction force and line width starts to break down, limiting the performance of FCP in this regime.
The open-loop conventional approach struggles to maintain the desired line width under disturbances in bed leveling, while FCP can consistently produce the desired line width.
The RMSE performance of the tuned FCP controller when printing a benchmark trajectory is 9.14 x 10^-3 N, which is 4.6% of the 0.2 N reference force.
The authors use a feed rate of 100 mm/s, a nozzle temperature of 300°C, a bed temperature of 170°C, and a nozzle diameter of 0.15 mm in their experiments.
The authors' custom-built Cartesian FFF machine has a maximum speed of 2 m/s, a maximum acceleration of 40 m/s^2, and an accuracy of 1 μm.
The authors use a Mellow Sherpa Micro extruder with an LDO-20-8T stepper motor, customized with their torque sensor configuration.
